utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone, Ms. Van Dusschoten and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, my name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel for Mr. Delalic is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, a professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honour, my name is Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic. My co-counsel is my colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. If it pleases the court, after consultation with my client, he has considerable difficulties with his eyes; therefore with the permission of this Trial Chamber if possible he would like to ask that during the trial he would like to have dark sunglasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honour, my name is Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo with Mr. Tom Moran, a lawyer from Houston Texas. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am John Ackerman and I appear here today along with Cynthia McMurray on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think I referred to Mr. Mucic's complaint. Is it dark glasses tendered for protecting his eyes from the light? If it makes him comfortable, there is nothing wrong with it. He can wear his dark glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. That is exactly due to the very strong light, so he has sore eyes and he feels much better if he is wearing dark glasses. I would like to thank your Honours for allowing my client to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the position with the witness, this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. As your Honours are aware we are halfway through the testimony of the witness Draganic and he is available to continue now, if that is convenient to your Honours. I might just at this stage indicate that we have had very great difficulties with witnesses, and considerable problems have arisen. We had intended to have -- there is Mr. Kuljanin, who is the next witness, and then after him there was to be Witness J, witness Zebic and witness Drezic. All three of those witnesses have refused to come to The Hague. Although we are endeavouring to persuade them otherwise, they at this stage simply refuse to come. We are in the process of trying to obtain another witness to come here, but whether we are successful in that is not something I can assure your Honours of, unfortunately, at this stage. As your Honours are aware, there are some outstanding legal arguments, particularly with documents. I do expect the legal argument in respect to the Austrian documents to be very lengthy in terms of consideration of each and every document, so it is possible that most of the time of this week could be devoted to that. It is not entirely a pleasant prospect, but that would take care of perhaps quite a bit of the time. We are endeavouring to obtain another witness, at least one more witness, to deal with that loss that we have had, so that is our current position. Your Honours had suggested we could have legal argument this morning on the question of the admissibility of the one document and handwriting sample that was the subject of a motion yet to be determined. I am not sure whether your Honours wish to deal with that before we complete the evidence of this witness, or whether your Honours would be prepared to permit this witness to complete his evidence and he can go home. He has been here all over the weekend, and as is the case with the other witness who will follow, has been here, in fact, your Honour, since Thursday week, so he has been here almost getting on towards a fortnight. Our position is that we would prefer to deal with the evidence, if that is possible, of the witnesses so they can go home, these two witnesses and then to deal with legal argument which we think will be lengthy and take us some time. If your Honours wish, we are in your Honours' hands as to which way you wish to deal with this. We could now proceed with legal argument, complete the evidence of the witness that is halfway through testifying; it is a matter for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I remember we mentioned the matter of taking the arguments with Mr. Greaves last week, it was to have them taken on Wednesday. Perhaps we should get through the witness which was on at that time, and I suppose Mr. Greaves might not be too strong in objecting if --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am well conscious of my learned friend's sound common sense in dealing with witnesses in that way, because obviously it falls into logical pieces instead of breaking things up with legal argument, then half a witness, then a whole witness, then legal argument again. That does not seem to me to be a very sensible way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is better with all the witnesses giving their evidence and then we will continue with the legal argument, both in your case and the other matter as well, so we are not perhaps breaking the arguments with witnesses in the middle. So when we start the legal arguments, we will continue with it and finish it, in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For a change I find myself in agreement with my learned friend. He should not count on it always though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am indebted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is a good arrangement. Let us carry on with the witness as we now have him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to present my view. This is something we have already discussed last week. We do agree with hearing two witnesses and then we want presentation of arguments, but if my colleagues from the Prosecution think that they should call some other witnesses, they should be heard only after we finish all the legal arguments, because we do not wish to be under any pressure of time when we present our arguments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I did not understand them to wish to call all witnesses before legal argument. All witnesses they have on the list and are available now are the ones they wanted to call. Not another witness who is not even around. Just the witnesses we have. RAJKO DRAGANIC (continued) Examined by MR. TURONE (continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, how are you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you remind the witness he is still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to remind you you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, last week before the break, you were testifying about Scepo Gotovac and more precisely about the second time he was called out of the hangar in the evening at about 9.00 pm. You said you heard screamings outside, then Gotovac was carried into the hangar again and that is where he died, you said. So now let me ask you: approximately how long did Gotovac remain outside this second time in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he stayed there for about 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who returned Gotovac into the hangar this second time in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was carried in by these two, by Todor and Novak Zelenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody invite these two prisoners to return Gotovac into the hangar on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were called by Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zenga there too? Did you see him being present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything else at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, he told him to go out. He could not go out so these two carried him. Later, he also called them to carry him inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did then Gotovac reach his position in the hangar, helped by these two prisoners, or was he in a position to move by himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he could not move himself. He was already dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean already dead or already almost dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost dead. He did not really live for more than five minutes after he got into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Gotovac brought again in the same position near you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was there, I mean across from me, next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you observe Gotovac and his body with some attention, either that night or the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We took him out the next morning, in the morning, when it dawned. Then we saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, could you observe his body with some attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the man was wearing a suit, he was a dead man. We did not really pay all that much attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see specific bruises, injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. That is asked and answered. He said he did not pay close attention to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He said he did not pay close attention to him. The question has already been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put your question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gotovac, do you remember if you saw any specific bruises or injuries or blood on Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, I mean the head was bruised, he had bruises on his body. I guess he did. I did not see it, but he was badly beaten up, you could see that, but he was wearing a suit so I could not really see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you notice that he died a few minutes after coming back into the hangar? How could you realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it, I mean I saw him going still, because it was not really dark, you could really -- there was still some daylight until 10.00. He stopped breathing. Branko Zelenovic and he also said "Scepo is dying, Scepo has just died". That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the following morning. Could you personally observe the following morning the body to remain motionless for a significant amount of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was lying there and then they came maybe around 10.00, 9.00 or 10.00. They carried him out and I do not know where they took him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who came and removed the body, Mr. Draganic? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Delic and Zenga there, he was taken out by the prisoners. They closed the door and I do not know where they took him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the last time you saw Gotovac or his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Already, thank you. Mr. Draganic, could you personally observe any other incident which led to the death of any prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I do not know which date it was exactly, they called up Simo Jovanovic, they called him up. They beat him up outside and they carried him into the hangar. It was night and naturally in the morning we saw him dead, he was lying there at his place. I mean, I heard that and I saw it. I know when they called him up, when they took him. Zenga called him up. He went outside and they hit him there. They beat him up and they also dragged him in, I do not know which ones were the ones who dragged him inside but he was there the next morning when it dawned they also came for him and they drove him away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you do not remember the date, but do you at least remember the month in which this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was the month of July, the month of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Zenga saying anything specific in this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He called Jovanovic up, he called up his name and he went outside, and something concrete I really do not know. I do not remember hearing anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did Jovanovic remain outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you hear from outside? Could you hear any noise coming from outside --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard blows and screaming and crying of a man while he had strength and then when it stopped, when he stopped screaming, then they called for someone to carry him inside. They carried him inside. When we saw him in the morning, he was dead and he was covered with an army coat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Jovanovic reach his position in the hangar by himself at that time when he was brought inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not. He was also carried inside by two prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember to which position inside the hangar was Jovanovic brought, his position inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also I mean where he was lying, I think it was in the fourth row from the door, somewhere in the middle of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask the Registry again to provide the witness again with Exhibit 174, the map of the hangar, please? Just let it be on the ELMO, please, with a pen or a pencil being provided to the witness. (Handed). Can you please, Mr. Draganic, mark with a circle the position of Mr. Jovanovic on this map and write "Jovanovic" just close to this circle. (Witness marks map). Thank you very much. Mr. Draganic, could you observe Mr. Jovanovic with some attention and describe him? Did you see specific bruises, specific injuries, any blood on him after he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning I saw it in the morning when it dawned, we all watched and he was bruised, his head was almost black, and we held his arms, his legs. He was really badly beaten, he obviously had broken bones. You could see that from a distance. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the body have any movement? Was it motionless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A dead body next to us, a dead stiff body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long could you observe the body remaining there motionless in the hangar before he was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we could see it in the morning as of 4.00 until 9.00 or 10.0, which was when they carried him away. I do not know, for five or six hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody order to remove the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came, but I really cannot say exactly now. They came and they said -- I do not know whether it was Delic or Zenga, I cannot remember everything now, but they just came, they carried the body outside and they drove it away. I do not know where they drove it away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the last time you saw the body of Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the last time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you personally observe any other incident which led to the death of any other prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Bosko Samoukovic. He was also sitting behind me in the fourth row against the wall, and Zenga was beating some prisoners from Bradina and then he called for Bosko and he beat him up. He forced him to do push-ups and he did push-ups and he was hitting him in the chest with his boot, with a rifle butt. Then there was a 7 by 10 plank and he hit him several times and the man fell. His sons were there as well, his two sons were in the camp. Then he ordered him to be taken out to fresh air. They took him or they carried him out and one of his sons went to the infirmary, to number 22, and when he came back, he said that his father had died, and I saw him then and that was the last time I ever saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how long did Bosko Samoukovic's beating last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was perhaps 10, 15 minutes. To me at the time it seemed very long. I do not know exactly how long it was. We were all there. It was in the hangar and all the prisoners saw it. That was not outside. Such beating and such humiliation and mistreatment, a person in his right mind would not be able to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, did Zenga say anything while beating Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did say, but I cannot really guess what he said because I cannot remember. He did say things, but I cannot say exactly what it was. But he did say things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did this incident happen, at least in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was also in July, July. It was probably around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Again, did you personally observe any other incident which led to the death of another prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well also when Zeljko Klimenta was killed, I was in the hangar, it was in the morning, I think it was 26th July 1992. The guard Padalovic called outside Ratko Cecez, Nenad Cecez and Kujundzic, nicknamed Gala. They were doling out food in the hangar, he called them to go outside. They left the hangar and Zeljko Klimenta asked whether he could go out as well. So he left the hangar, it was about 7.00 am and they were there. Then Kujundzic ran into the hangar and Cecez as well, he was holding his head, we asked what happened. There was a shot, we could hear a shot and he said Keljo got killed, so this is what I saw, this is what I heard actually. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After how long did you hear the shot outside after these people going outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they left about 5.00 and this happened around 7.00 am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these people you mentioned Kujundzic, Ratko Cecez et cetera, tell you anything more precise about how Klimenta was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there, and he said that he was joking, that he did not know he had a bullet in the Chamber and that he fired the shot as a joke. That is what I heard from them from talking to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he, who do you mean with he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean Padalovic, the guard. He said that he did not know he had a round in the Chamber, and that it was all an accident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, could you personally see after that which was the place where Klimenta was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the position towards the door of the hangar, I just saw them washing away the blood in the place where he was killed, but I did not see him because the door was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the hangar, maybe about 5 or 6 metres away from the hangar towards the guard post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Draganic, did you personally eyewitness any other mistreatment of any other prisoners while you were in hangar 6, even if it did not lead to the death of anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there when Mirko Babic was burned, when his trousers were burned by Zenga and he was not allowed to put the fire out. The fire was burning, the cloth was on fire and it caused burns on him. I was an eyewitness, I saw the burns, the horrible burns that he had. And I also saw various beatings and maltreatments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us focus on this incident concerning Mirko Babic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might object. I believe that the witness has said "I eyewitnessed the burns themselves". I would just ask that the Prosecutor be asked to lay the proper predicate as to whether he was an eyewitness to the actual event or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is exactly what I am going through, details about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you personally see Zenga doing to Mr. Mirko Babic, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that personally. I saw when he put his trousers on fire and he was not allowed to put it out, so it was on fire, it burned and normally caused burns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, did that happen inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say in detail how did Zenga put fire on Babic's trousers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took a match, lit the trousers and they were on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that done on one leg or both legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one leg. I saw it just on one leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the leg, the lower part of the leg below the knee or over the knee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lower part of the leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you could personally see his injuries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe this injury in detail? What do you see exactly on the leg of Mr. Mirko Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the leg of Mirko Babic I saw a very bad burn. I cannot really describe it, it looked like pine bark, it was black, the wound was black and it was covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this happened inside the hangar. Can you show to the court which position exactly inside the hangar, using the map on your right-hand side, please? Could you please mark on the map with a circle the position of Mirko Babic and write the name "Mirko Babic" right near this circle? Thank you very much. (Witness marks map). Mr. Draganic, can you say approximately when did this incident happen, at least in which month, if you remember, approximately? If you do not remember, never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in early July 1992, but I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mirko Babic receive any medical care after this incident, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not immediately, maybe a few days later. Delic brought some ointments which they put on the wounds, but not immediately then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zenga say anything during the incident itself, while putting fire on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did say something, but I cannot tell you now what it was because I cannot remember what he was saying. I did not pay much attention to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally eyewitness any other incident concerning any other prisoner while you were in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was also able to observe Spaso Miljevic. Zenga tortured him. He heated up the knife and made him hold the knife with his hands so he had blisters on his hands. That is what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you personally see the blisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He showed me, that prisoner showed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how did Zenga heat the knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He spilt some liquid on the concrete floor and set fire on it, and then he heated the knife in it and forced him to hold the knife in his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you again show to the court on the map on your right what the position of Spaso Miljevic, with a circle on that map, and just close to that write "Miljevic", please. (Witness marks map). Thank you very much. Can you say approximately when did all this happen, approximately at least the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well it was also July. I do not know the exact date, but it was in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Spaso Miljevic receive any medical care after this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, as far as you remember, did Zenga say anything during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. He was saying things that he was Arkan, that he was a volunteer -- he was saying lots of things. I really do not know. He was telling him things. I do not know anything specific, I just know that he was saying -- he was telling him that he was Arkan, that he would pay for everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any other incident, any mistreatment concerning any other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember the incident with Vukasin Mrkajic, where Zenga put a slow burning fuse and set it on fire and forced him to run around the hangar. He put it in his underwear and he was running and the fuse was burning. He was screaming, and then I think that Zenga pulled out the fuse out of his underwear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Zenga wrap the fuse around Vukasin Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He put it on the backside and pulled it to the other side and set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you personally see Vukasin's injuries from the fuse, if any injuries he received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not able to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, do you remember whether Zenga said anything during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was saying things. Vukasin was the chairman of the SDS for Bradina, so he was threatening him. I do not know the specific things that he told him. I cannot remember all the details now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any other incident, any other mistreatment of other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also remember the two brothers, Vaso and Veseljko Dordic. Mr. Delic was there also and they forced them to slap each other, to beat each other and then Zenga forced the two brothers to, if you will excuse me, this is really sad and humiliating, but I really saw that, they forced them to do something with their sexual organs. This is something that a normal human being could not do. This is really terrible, what they were doing. These were innocent people, and this was all done, they were maltreated for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, do not feel uncomfortable. Let us say exactly what they were forced to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to suck each others' penises, if you will excuse me, in front of everybody else, all of us in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did Veseljko and Vaso Dordic suffer any other mistreatment beside that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not Zenga who was -- actually Zenga was beating everybody all the time, he was kicking them. He was beating them with rifle buts, every time he would feel like it, he would come in and beat people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any relative of Veseljko and Vaso Dordic present in the hangar any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were relatives, Nebolsa, Dragisa, Gojko, there were quite a few relatives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the father of Veseljko and Vaso Dordic ever present in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their father was brought in on 12th July, I remember that, and he spent just one night there, and in the morning he was taken out of the camp and they remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who called the father of the two brothers out of the hangar when he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo came in the morning and he called him out and Jelenko left and never came back. His sons remained in hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Draganic, can you remember any other incident who you might have eyewitnessed while you were inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well there was Branko Gotovac, Zenga beat him very badly. Zenga was saying that -- recalling some incident when they were neighbours, so that this man was virtually almost dying, he was very sick and then Mr. Delic came and took Mr. Gotovac to the infirmary, to number 22 so he survived, he recovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything, any other incident you might remember concerning other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were incidents, Jovo Draganic was also beaten by Mr. Delic. He was beaten with a baseball bat. I do not know how he survived that. All those blows. There are many other details, and I cannot really recall all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a name by the name Dusan Bendzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot about that, Dusan Bendzo. Zenga also set his trousers on fire and he was burned. He beat him and he maltreated him. I do not know how he survived all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you personally see his injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe this injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was also a burn on his lower leg. The wound was blue and red, you know what a burn looks like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that also happen inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please show to the court with this map the position of Dusan Bendzo inside hangar 6 with a circle, writing the word "Bendzo" right near it. (Witness marks map). Your Honour, may I tender for admission Exhibit 174?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, just for clarification purposes could we have the witness draw the lines so we know which line that these people were seated in, just so we can tell perceptually where they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The seating arrangement, whether he can indicate the seating arrangement so we can be more exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If you can draw the lines, Mr. Draganic, in order to indicate the lines according to where the prisoners were sitting and so that it is clear to which lines all the marks you did belong. (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the second row, this is the third row and this is the fourth row.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Is 174 admitted, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Draganic, were you ever interrogated by military investigators while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated about three or four days. It was 18th or 20th June 1992 after we were brought in. That was when I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the camp were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Celebici command building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who called you out of the hangar in order to take you to the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A guard, I do not know who he was. He called out some of us, so we came to the command building, and he said we should lean against the wall and put our heads against the wall and to wait there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which wall are you talking about, Mr. Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The infirmary, building number 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said you were called out of the hangar with some other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from building number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but how many prisoners were called outside together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six of us, myself, Goran Draganic, Marinko Zivak, Jovo Draganic, Branko Zelenovic and Bozo Zivak, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these six prisoners who were called out of the hangar at the same time, were you the first who was interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Draganic was the first. I was the second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you stay while waiting for your turn to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were next to the infirmary, number 22. We were waiting there to be called in, and while we waited the man nicknamed Hodza called Goran Draganic out, they knew each other well, they went to school together and the rest of us continued waiting. While we waited I looked around and I saw a guard walking. He was holding some kind much an instrument and he beat everything once and when he came to me he did not beat me. Then we waited for a while and then Mr. Delic came and asked Jovo Draganic who was next to me, he asked "where is your beard and your song? You used to sing". He said, "you will pay for this". Then he left. Then the second time a guard came carrying a hammer, it was a wooden or a rubber hammer and he beat Marinko Zivak and he fell down. Again he did not beat me. Then after a while a third person came holding some kind of a bat and then he approached me, it was in summer and I was wearing a shirt, and he pulled up my shirt to my neck and he hit me twice on the back, so this finished and then I was called in, it was my turn and I was questioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, is what you describe right now happened while you were facing the wall of building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen while you were waiting for your turn, while Goran Draganic was being interrogated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mentioned the name of somebody called Hodza who called Goran Draganic to be interrogated. Do you know who is this person and what is the complete name of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him personally, his father was called Hodza, they lived in Bradina, I know him as well, but I do not know his exact name, his first and last names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your turn came, can you say who were the persons who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Hodza and two other people, two other men and a woman who was a secretary. I did not know many people in Konjic because I did not work there. I worked in the fields so I did not spend much time in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Were these people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated during the very interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me where I was for the past six months, what I was doing, whether I had weapons, who had given me the weapon and I answered all their questions; where you were, I said in Bradina, they asked me whether I had fired the weapon, I said no, and then they told me, "you are all saying that you do not know anything now" and he cursed my mother. That is all. They did not really question me much, so my statement was very brief. I said that I was in Libya, and that I had arrived on 28th April in 1992, that I had come home at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, can you say in which room of the command building were you interrogated? I mean, did the room face the camp or face the road outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the entrance of the command, down along the hallway, the last room on the right, that is where I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, did the window or windows of the room face the camp or face the road outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I honestly cannot say. I was not really paying attention to that. I just do not know. If I was on the right-hand side, we were facing the street, and not the camp, towards the town of Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we show you a model of the command building, would you be in a position to indicate the very room where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness the enlarged model of the command building, so the big building under there. Just turn it the other side --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just going to have to ask the court's indulgence, because this was so long ago these models were placed before us. If my memory serves me correctly, I believe that model was not introduced into evidence because they could not verify that it was accurate in any way. I know the model of the camp itself was but I believe this model was not introduced at that time. I may be wrong, but that is what I remember. That was back in early March. Is there some way that we can verify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I think I remember that we had a second witness, Mr. Broubils, after Mr. Bellen who introduced this model 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really cannot remember that. I do remember there was a controversy over that one model. I will leave it up to your memory as to what you remember about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually it depends upon the purpose for which it is now being used. If it is only to indicate where the witness stayed and if he could give the bearing from where he could see things, perhaps it might be mutually useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe it could be. I think our objection back then was that if they could not authenticate that it was accurate, then it could not be used for demonstrative purposes because then the person would be thrown off. I will leave it up to the court. I just vaguely remember something eight months ago that dealt with that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I remind my learned colleague of the Defence that actually this model was admitted through the second witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The second witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I accept Mr. Turone's explanation as true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the door, the entrance of the building, Mr. Draganic? If you take out the roof of the building, could you please indicate to the court, as far as you remember, which was the room in which you were interrogated? You can stand up if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this room here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The room has a number. May the usher say the number which appears in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12, here. THE USHER: 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Draganic, it does not -- it is all right, thank you. We have finished with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If I might just ask that we have a number for that exhibit so I can mark it in my notes to be more accurate, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Provide the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 2B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Draganic, did you sign any piece of paper, any record after the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry. Mr. Draganic, did you sign any piece of paper, any record after that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really remember whether I signed anything or not. I did give a statement, but whether I signed it or not, it is possible that I did, but I just cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from signing, do you remember having read, anything written concerning your statement or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not read it, nor was it given to me to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the interrogation? Did you have to remain outside again, against the wall, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did stay against the wall and then when we were finished the guards took us to the hangar, to number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten again while --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did the Red Cross ever visit the camp during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did in July. I was there and that was when we were registered. When the Red Cross came, we were allowed to say what our problems were without the presence of the guards. Then in the evening when the Red Cross left, then eight guards came and Delic and Zenga were there and then we were beaten up, because we had said perhaps what was happening in the camp or something like that and maybe they saw it and that is when we were beaten and mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other time when the Red Cross came, or only once, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice more while I was in the camp, but I cannot remember the exact dates, because on 30th August I was released to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the other occasions when the Red Cross came, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing really happened. Later it was better, the food was better and they were not beating us as much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the occasion on which you were beaten after the first visit you have been talking about, did the guards say anything while beating you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, somebody from Foca then again somebody from Modric, Kumdic that was his name, four of them, it was done very quickly, like in films, I was kicked on both sides, I was hit. I really thought I would not survive something like that. I have survived everything and then they went on, they beat people up very quickly and then they just left the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides this, besides what you said already, did you personally suffer any other beating or physical maltreatment during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only once Mr. Delic hit me, kicked me here and when we were going outside to the toilet we had to run, and on my way back, the rope holding my trousers was undone. I started laughing because my trousers almost fell down and I did not see Delic inside, so I sat down to my place and then all of a sudden there was somebody's foot here. He swore at me and I did not know what to say, because my trousers were falling down and then after that I was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what did Mr. Delic beat you in that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He kicked me. He was wearing boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know Delic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Zenga from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know Zenga either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which role did you observe Delic having in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. We called him Mr. Commander, but exactly what his role was, I do not know. He knows, but I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of who was Mr. Delic's superior inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, he has described Mr. Delic as Mr. Commander. That implies that he is the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let us rephrase the question. Do you know who was the superior of Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Mr. Pavo, Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the role of Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They used to say that he was the camp commander, but that I do not know. He used to come there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many times did you see Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him perhaps on ten occasions during the time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say in which parts of the camp did you see him and doing what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, an Arab TV crew, I think, was visiting us and there were about ten of them, the crew and Pavo, Delic and some others, and they asked some people about their -- about what was happening. They asked Zeljko what his treatment was and he naturally said certain things, but there were naturally certain things that he did not dare say, as things were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic usually wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well he was wearing trousers with pockets and he had a T-shirt and he had an automatic gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mucic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, when did you finally leave Celebici camp? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: An objection, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said 30th August, if I remember correctly. If I remember correctly, he said 30th August.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honour, you are right. I am sorry. This is the end, but your Honour, just for the record to be clear, since we did not clarify that when the witness pointed the area of the manholes on the model, and since there is not really a sticker in that area, may I be allowed to ask the witness this last question? Mr. Draganic, can you say approximately in which part of the camp were the manholes you have been talking about during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where to show you? On the map?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you showed us on the map, but can you say, just describe with your own words approximately in which part of the camp the manhole area was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can use the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You can point again to the model if you wish and say where the area was, close to what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There, the manholes are there (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My problem is that there is not a sticker any more on that area. It used to be. For the record, I would like to make clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Does anything there show manholes? Does anything there demonstrate that there are manholes there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There is a number of small squares.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, but I could not really observe that because I was not really allowed to look while they were taking us there. I had to look straight ahead, I could not really have a close look at things to really observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Anyway, just for the record, let us say that he pointed at an area which is not far from the gate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How then do we identify it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just behind tunnel number 9.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just behind tunnel number 9, as Judge Jan says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If there is anyone who has talked about manholes, then we should identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I did not get you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not understand that this is the only witness who has spoken about manholes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Then I think we pointed out for the record that he indicated an area right behind tunnel 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If that satisfies you as the Prosecution, we can rely on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I think so, your Honour. This is the end of my examination-in-chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to inform you that Defence for Mr. Delalic has no questions for this witness. The cross-examination will be Mucic's Defence counsel, Defence counsel for Mr. Delic and finally Defence counsel for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour as for Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, we also have no questions for this witness. As far as we are concerned, this would complete our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to say I have no questions, but in fact I do. Let me go and get wired up down here. May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed. Cross-examined by MR. MORAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draganic -- or I guess it is good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and I am Hazim Delic's lawyer. I am going to ask you some questions, some of which are going to be directly related to what you have already talked about and some of which may have something to do with your statement, some which may not be anything you have talked about at all. I would like to ask you if we could have a deal, that you will listen to my questions and if you do not understand them, stop me and I will rephrase it so that you do understand it. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would listen to my questions and just answer the question that I ask, I think we -- some of them just call for yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that will get us out of here a lot quicker. Another thing is you have been nodding and you have also answered out loud. I would like to point out that there are two ladies in the courtroom, court reporters, and they have to write down anything any of us say. They cannot write down a nod. If you answer in words? Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that is great, sir. Thank you very much. The first thing I would like to talk to you about is the military actions that you were involved in. I understand that you had a M48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 48, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a military rifle, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It fires, what, 7.62 millimetre military round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is designed to shoot people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is what, a bolt action rifle, is it not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Do you have to work the action every time you fire a shot; is that not right, sir? Lift the bolt and pull it back and put it forward by hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is what we would call a bolt action rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it when I came back from Libya, around 6th, 5th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have to pay for it or did someone give it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given the gun, and I was told, "you should have it, you need it to defend your home". I did not really think I would need it for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you in any kind of a military unit with a commander or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there was really no commander. If there was a commander perhaps things would have happened differently. We were simply a village. We simply got together to prevent things. We went to the town community to negotiate. We prepared minutes of 10th May that we would leave each other alone, because in my village there were only Muslims and Serbs but as soon as the minutes were signed, perhaps after two hours, as soon as we returned, there was already an attack and that is when we fled, the younger people, younger women all fled to Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so -- you did not have any kind of uniform or badges or anything to show you were in some kind of a military unit, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing, I had nothing. I was in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, you were a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were citizens of Yugoslavia. I was a Yugoslav. We were all Yugoslavs until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that is fine, sir. Let me go on to something else. Let me jump forward to when you arrived at the Celebici camp, okay? You were on that truck --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- about 65 of you, 64, 65 prisoners taken off the truck and made to stand against this wall; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were a whole lot of guards around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were, but I honestly do not remember how many, because we were not allowed to look. I did not dare look, I did not look. They were there, but I really do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir and I understand that under those circumstances you could not count them. Could you help me out on this, were there just a few, was there a whole lot of them, or was it somewhere in between? Can you give me an approximate number, that is what I am asking for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe something like that, maybe 10, 15. I really do not know. Maybe there were more, I really cannot remember. I cannot say precisely because I did not dare look at them so I did not see so I am not able to say what the exact number was, because I simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that sir. No one is pressing you for an exact number. You could not count them. Did you get any feel for what their mood was? Was it a nasty mood, did they appear to be well behaved troops? How did they appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. We were standing against the wall for a while and then we were told to take everything out of our pockets. We did so and then after that, I really do not remember. I was not beaten when I was standing against the wall. I do not know about the others, they were not beating people standing next to me. Then we had to take our belts out, our shoelaces out. I was one of the first and the first seven, I was one of them, who were taken to the manholes. I really do not know what happened later after we left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I was asking about was did you have any feel for the demeanour and the mood of most of the soldiers that were there? Did they -- were they shouting at you and threatening you, or were they talking to you in a slow, clear, calm voice? What was the atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For them it was merry. For us it was sad. There were playing Gusle, a national Serb instrument and they told us all kinds of things, I really cannot remember, to be quite honest. But there was mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I am asking this, sir, is I am going to suggest something to you and maybe you can help me out with this. Let me suggest to you -- let me preface it with this. There has been a lot of testimony from others who were brought in in other groups that when they were standing at that wall they were beaten. Will you accept that from me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see, I think not, because I think we were okay compared to others, we people from Brdjani, because no one from my village was really tortured. We did not really give any resistance. We simply surrendered our weapons when we came back from Bradina. I think they were okay towards us, to people from Brdjani. I can only really say just the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I am suggesting to you is this: I am suggesting to you that Mr. Delic and some of the other guards hustled you away from the wall and put you down the manhole to protect you from other people, to keep you from being beaten. Do you have any indication if that is in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. Maybe. It is possible. I really do not know how to answer this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us step ahead. You were taken from the wall to the manhole and you were there for, what, in that manhole, about two hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there from noon or 1.00 in the afternoon until 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, about six hours, give or take a little. When you were brought out of the manhole, were there the same guards that were around when you were up against the wall, were they still there or had they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to the command around 7. Delic was there, he told us to go out. He opened the manhole, we all left and we had to put our hands on our heads and then we went to hangar number 6, we had to line up against the wall and then we were taken in in groups of five and he told each one of us exactly where to sit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but was there that large number of guards there, those guards that were laughing and having a good time when you were up against the wall, or had those people left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there? What do you mean, where? When they brought us to number 6, is that what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What I am asking, to cut right to the chase, is this: you have testified that there were a large number of guards when you were up against the wall and that they were kind of making merry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that what you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the manholes, there were six of us or seven of us in the manhole where I was and in the other manholes where other people were, Mirko Zivak and Zelenovic, they cried for help, they had asthma and had not enough air. So the guards took them out later and the rest of us left the manholes at around 7.00. Then all of us gathered together and went to the hangars. The guards were there when we were in manholes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they better behaved when you got out than they were when standing against the wall? Behaving more professionally, quieter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were quiet when we got out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that was what we were trying to get at. I appreciate it very much your helping me with that. Let me jump forward again a little bit to your interrogation. While you were in the camp, did you ever see or get to know the person who was the camp's driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the driver who drove the van, I know him by sight, but I do not know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I gave you a name, could that possibly ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible. It might.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you want to do this in closed session? The name has been mentioned in public session, it has been mentioned in closed session. Whatever pleases the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will do it in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour. Can we go into closed session for about 30 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let us go into closed session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay, we return to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, did you see that man when you were taken to be interrogated? Was he one of the people that took you over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I do not know who were the people who took us there. I cannot say that. There were some guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that is fine. Were your hands tied at any point while you were being interrogated or being led to the interrogation or being led back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That is fine, sir. Zeljko Klimenta, his death. When the guard -- after he was shot, you said the guard had said that he did not know the gun was loaded, basically; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the story was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see him, sir, the guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the guard later. He was there. He was guarding us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after the shooting was it that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Mr. Padalovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him immediately after that when they went out to hose down the blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what was his demeanour? Was he crying, was he laughing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he look like, sir? What was his demeanour? Did he look sad, did he look shocked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not happy. He was not laughing. He was depressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that is fine. Thank you very much, sir. Jovo Draganic, his beating. You testified about that. First let me ask you, is he any relative of yours, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you related to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe three times removed. It is really very distant relation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you close to him personally? Were you and he close friends? Did you see him a lot before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to see him, but we did not spend much time together because my house was closer to Podorasac than to Brdjani and since I did field work we did not see each other often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine. You testified that he was beaten by Mr. Delic with a baseball bat. Do you recall that maybe 30 minutes ago, an hour ago you testified to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you it was a baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw the bat. He carried the bat with him. It was a yellow bat and it had the word "Turbo" written on it. Nobody told me that, that is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I say that is that in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor you described it as a plank painted yellow as opposed to a baseball bat, and I am curious where the words "baseball bat" got into your vocabulary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used the term "Turbo bat", I just saw the baseball bat. I had never seen such a bat before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although baseball may be the national sport of my country, I am sure it is not of yours. I can understand why you would not see a baseball bat very often. How hard did Mr. Delic hit your cousin? Was it real hard when he hit him with that baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He hit him outside. He called him out and he beat him there outside. When he left we heard the blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not really know whether it was Mr. Delic or who hit him if it was outside; you did not see it, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that. I did not see it, because he beat him outside. He told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so the source of your information is your cousin. When you talked to the Prosecutor, the investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor -- strike that, let me back off for a second. You said you could hear the beatings, the blows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they real loud inside? Clearly you could hear them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that they were awfully hard blows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were. We changed his clothes and if you will excuse me, he was all wet, so his clothes were changed after he was brought in the hangar, and then later, I saw when his skin started to peel off. That is what I saw with my own eyes. I did not see the beating, but I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, about how long -- I know you did not have a watch so you cannot tell me exactly, but about how long did it take for this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time. It is an eternity. Maybe 20 minutes, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What parts of his body were bruised when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this part downwards (indicates). From the belt down, from the waist down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was both of his legs, his back, all over the entire lower part of his body from his belt down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Office of the Prosecutor's investigator that he was hit about 170 times, that is 170. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was 170 times. When you are expecting something, it seems like an eternity. He said himself that he was hit that many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You heard the hits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would 170 to 200 hits be an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not 200, maybe 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 170, just like he told the investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honour, somewhere we have in evidence a baseball bat. I would like to show it to the witness, unless it is still back in a closet some place. It is a Delic exhibit. (Handed). Sir, does that look something like what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is similar to this one, the bat was similar to this one, only it was wider and yellow and it tapered off and it had the word "Turbo" written on it. Whether it was of hard metal or of some other material I do not know, because I never held it in my hands. It just had the word "Turbo" written on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is Delic exhibit -- I believe 9.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D6/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That is all we need with the bat. Thank you very much. Sir, I am still troubled with the fact that when you talked to the Prosecutor you described that object as a plank and now you are describing it as a baseball bat, because like you said, you had never seen a baseball bat presumably before today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw it then, and I said that he beat Bosko Samoukovic with a plank. I did not say that for Jovo Draganic. I used the words "baseball bat".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you talked to -- who have you talked to about your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one? Let us go back in time. Before you got on the stand, I guess it was last Thursday, since you have gotten to The Hague have you talked to anybody from the Prosecutor's office, perhaps Mr. Turone, that nice gentleman that was asking you questions. Did you ever talk to him about your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so you talked to him. About how long was that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay besides Mr. Turone, and I presume an interpreter, was there anyone else present during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what that person's name is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You just had that one conversation with him, what, last week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have not talked to him about the case since then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those three people, Mr. Turone, the interpreter and whoever that other person was are the only three people in The Hague that you have talked to about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you came to The Hague, who did you talk to about your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked to Desa Vokmen. She invited me to come here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is she, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Desa Vokmen, that is her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is she associated with any groups, for instance, the Association of Detainees in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I honestly do not know, because I am not a member of the association, so I cannot talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But she talked to you about your testimony here. Who else was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
